tei:titleStmt.tei:title: עַל הַנִּסִּים בִּימֵי הוֹדָיָה לְאֻמִּיִּים
Al haNissim prayer on Civic Days of Patriotic Gratitude, by Aharon Varady

tei:div.tei:head: Al haNissim prayer on Civic Days of Patriotic Gratitude, by Aharon Varady

tei:lg.tei:l: “I am YHVH, I make all, I stretch out the heavens alone, the Earth is spread out before me with none beside me!”
I am the one who planted this Tree [of Life] in order that all the world should delight in it.
And in it, I spread all (kōl). I called it “all” because all depend on it, all emanate from it, and all need it.
To it they look, for it they wait, and from it, souls fly in joy.
Alone was I when I made it. Let no angel rise above it and say, “I was before you.”
I was also alone in the time when I spread out my Earth, in which I planted and rooted this Tree [of Life].
I made them rejoice together, and I rejoiced in them.
And for the miracles,
and for the redemptions,
and for the mighty acts,
and the rescues,
and the wonders,
that you made in this land
in those days, in this season,
in the face of war and massacre, terror and resistance.
For whom is the Earth’s land to seize and to occupy‽!
Speak to the Earth and she will teach you!
For you (Hashem) and not for us,
is the Earth and the fullness thereof.
Adam and Ḥavah were knit together in the womb,
within the innermost depths of Adamah (the Earth),
and we were only born as children of the Earth
to cultivate and preserve her Garden
with compassion for all of her living creatures.
“The Garden of Eden, where is it (now)?
Rabbi Amorai explained to them: ba-Arets (In the Earth).”
As immigrants in a foreign land,
we saw ourselves
as grasshoppers in the eyes of predatory overlords. —
“Not by their own sword did they seize land and possess it,
nor did their own arm save them,” (Psalms 44:4)
but “through your own hand (HaShem),
were the nations driven out and planted in;
you separated the peoples and spread them abroad” (Psalms 44:3).
And so as predator and prey
we were fed upon one another.
Consequently, the Earth screams silently
from the blood of our fellows it cannot help but soak up,
while we cry with gratitude
for the bounty and sanctuary we have found in her.
Meanwhile, we dare not look at each other’s faces —
how long will we hide our face from one another in shame?
Majestic King of all kings,
creator of all and sustainer of every burrow and dwelling:
as immigrants in a new land,
you elevated our ancestors, Avraham and Sarah, who welcomed every guest.
You commanded us to welcome the foreigner and stranger among us,
to redeem the captive, and to pursue justice.
You forbade us to steal and murder,
and required us to alleviate the suffering of any living creature in our midst.
You elevated us to champion your light among the nations.
Even as we were separated and spread abroad,
we wrote down your word and kept your Torah/Teaching,
we strove to make a home for you in this world of predation
with acts of kindness and prayers of thanksgiving.
May we ever be grateful for our shelter
and to strive with compassion for justice and peace
in every land that we dwell.
Blessed is the One who preserves the Earth for those who share in her bounty.

tei:note.tei:p: Isaiah 44:24, pronounced, roka ha’arets may-iti (the earth is spread out before me), but written roka ha’arets mi-iti מי אתי? (the earth is spread out. Who was with me?)
Each nation of the Earth has its respective angel called a Sar, literally “prince.” Let no national pride or spirit assume predominance.
Sefer HaBahir §22. Per §21, this exposition is from Rebbi Yoḥanan.
cf. Psalms 24:1, cf. Psalm 50:11, and Deuteronomy 10:14. This land is not yours, and it is not mine. The land is the Garden of HaShem.
cf. Genesis 2:15, l’ovdah ul’shomrah. We are commanded to be responsible stewards of this Garden, the earth’s biosphere.
cf. R’ Moshe Cordovero, Tomer Devorah, chapter three “On Ḥokmah (Supernal Wisdom)“.
Sefer haBahir §31. Surprisingly, the idea that the Garden of Eden was literally hidden in the Earth, can be found in the fairy tale recounted by Hans Christian Andersen, “The Garden of Eden.”

Numbers 13:33. Seeing oneself as an underling should not validate excuses for conquest or privilege. By grasshoppers, the verse suggests that the Bnei Anak, the giant children of the Nephilim, see newcomers as fast food, i.e., easy pickings. The Nephilim first referenced in Genesis ch. 6, are the bnei elohim — children of G‽D — who descend to Earth, take what they wish, and with their children, introduce predation into nature. Thematically, the Nephilim and their children are archetypal of any group or person who makes themselves into an oppressive bigshot.

My central point here is that a humanity that is not acting as a proper steward of the Earth (as the Garden of Hashem) cedes the role of “gardener” to G‽Δ who, as the one god of both suffering and joy, drives out, spreads, and plants humanity in a manner that might seem just as arbitrary and capricious to us as a human farmer ploughing and planting might seem to the wild creatures of the fields and forests.

from Genesis 4:10. Either the dahm (blood) of Kayin’s brother Abel cries out from Adamah (the earth) or the Adamah itself cries out. HaShem loves the Earth, and the Earth is ever burdened with the sins that humans cannot bear — and HaShem takes note.

cf. Psalms 126. As we should, but we need to reciprocate for our gratefulness by taking responsibility for our actions and the errors of the generations who came before us that acted with callous ignorance and neglect of the systems supporting life on earth and the welfare of the creatures we share this world with.
A reference to the umbrella mitsvah of tsaar baalei ḥayyim, being mindful not to cause the unnecessary suffering of all living creatures.
